nameStory: Smith's cress gets its name from English botanist Sir James Edward Smith, who founded the Linnean Society of London in the late 1700s. This little mustard family member was named in his honor, recognizing his contributions to botanical science. The 'cress' part of the name refers to its peppery taste, shared with other edible members of the mustard family.
description: Smith's cress is a small annual herb in the mustard family that typically grows 6-18 inches tall. It has a branching stem with small white flowers clustered at the top and leaves that vary in shape - some deeply lobed, others more oval. Like other mustard family plants, it produces tiny seed pods and has a slightly peppery smell when crushed. This European native is quite rare in New England, with only a handful of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Variable leaf shapes on the same plant - lower leaves are often deeply lobed like tiny oak leaves, while upper leaves are more oval and smooth-edged. Feel slightly fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in small clusters at stem tips. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across, and they have a faint sweet scent.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flat, round seed pods about 1/8 inch wide that feel papery when ripe. They're notched at the tip and contain just one or two seeds each.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading plant that branches from the base, forming small patches. Stems feel somewhat stiff and have a slightly hairy texture.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Crush a leaf between your fingers and you'll smell a mild peppery, mustard-like scent - characteristic of the mustard family.

habitat: Smith's cress grows in disturbed soils like waste areas, cultivated fields, and along roadsides. In its native Europe, it's found on shingle beaches and rocky areas, suggesting it tolerates poor, well-drained soils. In New England, look for it in coastal areas and urban environments where the soil has been disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants begin growing, with the characteristic variable leaves becoming visible by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Plants flower from early to mid-summer, producing their tiny white four-petaled blooms. Peak identification time when flowers and developing seed pods are both present.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open to release seeds. Plants begin to yellow and die back as cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring. No above-ground parts remain.

funFact: This tiny plant is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 6 times across all six states - making it one of the most elusive members of the mustard family in our region, despite being common as a weed in parts of Europe!
confusionNotes: Smith's cress can be confused with other small pepperweeds, but its variable leaf shapes on the same plant are distinctive - look for the combination of deeply lobed lower leaves and smooth upper leaves. Most other pepperweeds have more consistent leaf shapes throughout the plant.
contextualKnowledge: As a European introduction, Smith's cress represents one of many mustard family plants that have crossed the Atlantic with human activity. However, unlike some of its relatives that became common weeds, this species has remained extremely rare in North America.
compareHints: Smith's cress differs from its peppergrass relatives by having distinctly different leaf shapes on the same plant - deeply cut lower leaves and smooth upper ones. Virginia pepperweed has consistently toothed leaves throughout, while field peppergrass has more uniformly shaped, densely hairy leaves. The round, single-seeded pods also help distinguish it from some relatives that have larger or differently shaped seed pods.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia pepperweed differs from its peppergrass cousins mainly in its seed pods and leaves.
Among the pepperweeds, field peppergrass stands out with its forking flower branches and arrow-shaped stem leaves that clasp without leaf stalks.

Broadleaved pepperweed stands out from its pepperweed relatives by being much taller (3-6 feet vs 1-2 feet), having wider leaves, and forming large perennial colonies rather than growing as individual annual plants.
Unlike its upright pepperweed relatives like Virginia pepperweed and field peppergrass, lesser swine-cress grows in flat mats rather than standing erect.
Among the pepperweeds in New England, common peppergrass stands out for its notably hairy, grayish appearance and densely packed seed clusters.
Unlike Virginia pepperweed and field peppergrass which have similar leaves throughout the plant, clasping pepperweed has dramatically different leaf shapes from bottom to top.
Among its pepperwort relatives, narrow-leaved pepperwort stands out for having the thinnest, most finely divided leaves - much more thread-like than Virginia pepperweed or field peppergrass.
